title: work-queue-dequeue-lag-and-node-hotspot-scratchpad
body:
Summary:

This is a working scratchpad for the incident observed on 2026-03-10 where pod start p95 increased from ~1.2s to >20s for a subset of pods and scheduler workqueue dequeue latency spiked concurrently. Impact was ~18% of cluster pods experiencing delayed scheduling across two AZs for ~45 minutes.

High-level hypothesis:
- A small set of nodes entered a 'hotspot' state (high kernel CPU and conntrack churn) while kube-scheduler worker threads were slowed by long-running processing of several heavy predicate/priority checks and cache invalidation storms. That produced long dequeue times in the scheduler workqueue which cascaded into scheduling backpressure across cluster.

How we detected it:
- Alerts: p95 pod startup >10s (alert fired at 08:42 UTC), scheduler-dequeue-p95 >500ms (alert fired at 08:44 UTC)
- Grafana: scheduler_queue_dequeue_latency_seconds p95 jumped from 0.05s to 2.1s for ~40 minutes
- Node metrics: two nodes (ip-10-20-34-12, ip-10-20-41-239) show sustained system_cpu_usage > 88% and softirq spikes correlated with network RX/TX packets per second
- Conntrack: established conntrack entries for the two nodes grew by ~6x in 10m window (conntrack_count metric)
- kubelet logs: repeated pod eviction/restart churn on the hotspot nodes around 08:35 UTC (OOM or DiskPressure flaps not present; more of start/stop churn)

Initial timeline (UTC):
- 08:32: monitoring: small increase in pod start p95 noted by alerting rule in staging/cluster
- 08:42: alerting threshold breached -> oncall page
- 08:44: scheduler dequeue latency alert
- 08:45: SRE oncall (Aisha) began triage; triage channel created #sre-scheduler-dequeue
- 08:48: Confirmed two nodes with elevated kernel CPU and conntrack growth
- 08:52: Temporary mitigation: cordon one hotspot node and drain low-priority workloads
- 09:02: dequeue latency p95 decreased to ~0.2s after draining node and evicting noisy workloads
- 09:18: uncordon/slow rollout of evicted pods across AZ and node pools with autoscaler assistance
- 09:45: incident declared resolved; post-incident notes capture started

Investigation notes and evidence:
- kubectl top node for ip-10-20-34-12 showed CPU 91% and memory 62%
- dmesg on node: repeated messages about nf_conntrack table wrap/timeout entries (sampling): "nf_conntrack: table full, dropping" around 08:37
- iptables ruleset size increased due to ephemeral host-networked daemonset pods creating many rules (auditlogs show calico-policy-hook bumping rules)
- kube-scheduler logs: frequent "Operation executor took Xms" entries where X climbed into hundreds of milliseconds for predicate evaluation loops (predicates touching NodeAffinity + podAntiAffinity + resource checks)
- Metrics snapshot: etcd request latency did not increase significantly (p50/p95 stable), so contention is localized to scheduler/node kernel interactions rather than control plane throttling

Root cause analysis (working):
1) Primary: Network/conntrack pressure on two nodes caused high kernel CPU and packet processing interrupts (softirq), starving userland scheduler processes on those nodes for timely kubelet heartbeats and nodestatus updates. That increased scheduler churn trying to re-evaluate many pending pods and causing workqueue dequeue stalls.
2) Contributory: A recent rollout introduced a hostNetwork daemonset (experimental) that creates ephemeral iptables chains per pod which scaled with ephemeral workload count; that amplified conntrack churn and rule processing overhead.
3) Contributory: Scheduler logic (custom predicate ordering) included an expensive anti-affinity check for the affected podtypes. When node status updated rapidly, scheduler re-enqueued many items causing queue pressure.

Immediate mitigations applied:
- Cordon + drain ip-10-20-34-12 (08:52) and ip-10-20-41-239 (08:56) to stop new workloads landing on hotspots.
- Scaled up dedicated worker node pool (non-hostNetwork) by +2 to absorb eviction traffic and reduce scheduling backlog.
- Rolled back the experimental hostNetwork daemonset (08:58) to reduce iptables churn; confirmed conntrack growth stabilized after rollback (~08:59).
- Increased kube-scheduler log level to debug for 10 minutes to capture predicate latencies (done at 08:50).

Commands run during triage (snippets):
- kubectl get nodes -o wide | egrep "34-12|41-239"
- kubectl describe node ip-10-20-34-12
- sudo cat /proc/net/nf_conntrack | wc -l  # used on node for quick conntrack count (run via bastion)
- sudo iptables -L -n -v | wc -l  # to see rule explosion
- kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-scheduler-xyz --since=15m | grep "operation took" | sed -n '1,200p'

Post-incident follow-ups (action items):
- Short term (owner: Jonah Kim, due 2026-03-17): add a guardrail in deployment CI that prevents hostNetwork daemonsets from being rolled into large clusters without SRE sign-off and approval.
- Medium term (owner: Diego Morales, due 2026-04-01): add a scheduler metric and alert that tracks "predicate loop time per item" (expose histogram of predicate durations) and set runbook guidance for p95 thresholds.
- Medium term (owner: Priya Sharma, due 2026-04-08): add conntrack growth anomaly alert scoped by node and by AZ with automated remediation suggestions (cordon/drain step-runbooks).
- Runbook edits (owner: Aisha Patel, due 2026-03-20): update "node-hotspot" runbook with items below and add a checklist for hostNetwork/iptables-related debug steps.

Runbook draft additions (to be merged):
- Detection:
  - Query: sum by(node) (increase(rate(node_network_rx_packets_total[5m]))) > relative_baseline -> candidate hotspot nodes
  - Query: conntrack_count{node="$node"} > 0.8 * conntrack_max_entries -> raise node-conntrack-pressure alert
- Triage steps:
  1) ssh to node via bastion, check /proc/net/nf_conntrack count and dmesg for "table full" messages
  2) run sudo iptables -S | wc -l to estimate rules; correlate with hostNetwork daemonset counts
  3) if kernel softirq > 50% for >5m and conntrack high -> cordon & drain
  4) identify and rollback any recent hostNetwork/privileged rollouts (kubectl rollout history / check CI annotated deploys)
- Mitigation playbook:
  - If cordon+drain reduces scheduler latency, keep node cordoned and schedule maintenance window to cycle kernel or reprovision node; otherwise isolate and escalate to infra
  - If many nodes show similar symptoms across AZ, scale cluster control plane (not observed in this incident)

Open questions (for post-mortem):
- Why did the hostNetwork daemonset create per-pod iptables chains rather than a shared chain? (owner: platform-engineering)
- Can we add better isolation or cgroup tuning to reduce kernel-level packet processing impact on userland scheduler threads?

Appendix: notable logs and metric snippets (redacted)
- scheduler log sample: "I0310 08:46:30.123456 1 factory.go:XXX] predicate evaluation took 245ms for pod/xzy"
- node dmesg sample: "nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet" (multiple repeats 08:36-08:40)
- quick grafana links: cluster/queue-latency-dashboard (p95) and node/conntrack-growth-view

Notes on prevention and capacity: 
- Increase conntrack_max on large instance types by default for nodepool images where hostNetwork workloads are allowed (requires kernel tuning and will be audited).
- Consider a mutating admission controller that forbids hostNetwork usage for small ephemeral pods to avoid per-pod rule scoping.

Conclusion (working):
This was primarily a node-level networking pressure problem that manifested as scheduler workqueue overload. The immediate mitigations (cordon/drain + rollback of hostNetwork daemonset) restored steady-state. Next steps are CI guardrails, runbook enhancements, and adding targeted metric alerts for predicate latency and per-node conntrack growth.

(End of scratchpad)
